questions.title: What a flowchart is
questions.text: Which statement best describes a **flowchart**?

options.content: A diagram of how data moves between the processes, data stores and external entities of a system
A diagram that shows the steps of one process in order, using standard symbols joined by arrows
A table listing every field of a database with its data type
A list of the hardware needed to run a system

scheme.explanation: A flowchart shows how one process works step by step. Option A describes a DFD; C is a data dictionary.

questions.title: DFD or flowchart

options.content: To show which external entities send data to the system
To show how one process works step by step, including its decisions and loops

To show the network the system will run on

scheme.explanation: A DFD shows what processes exist and how data flows; a flowchart shows how each process works, so it can be coded.

questions.title: Terminator shape
questions.text: START and END are drawn in a rectangle, because they are processes.

scheme.explanation: START and END use the terminator — a rounded rectangle (oval). A plain rectangle is for a calculation or assignment.

Steps carried out one after another, each once
A decision chooses one of two paths

questions.title: Cinema price
questions.text:
A flowchart inputs a customer's `age`. Decision: `age < 12?` — Yes: `price ← 1500`; No: `price ← 2500`. Then `OUTPUT price`.

State the output when the age entered is **12**.

scheme.explanation: 12 < 12 is false, so the No exit is followed: price = 2500. 12 is a boundary value.

questions.text:
A student's flowchart: START (oval) → `INPUT price` in a **rectangle** → diamond `price > 5000?` with **one** exit arrow labelled Yes → `discount ← price × 0.1` (rectangle) → `OUTPUT price − discount` (parallelogram), and no END symbol.

Select the **three** errors.

options.content: INPUT price should be in a parallelogram
The calculation should be in a parallelogram
The decision needs a second exit labelled No
The output should be in a diamond

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and E. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Input uses a parallelogram, every decision needs two labelled exits, and the flowchart must end with an END terminator. The calculation in a rectangle and the output in a parallelogram are correct.

questions.title: Advantages of flowcharts
questions.text: Select the **two** advantages of designing a process with a flowchart.

options.content: The logic can be followed visually, even by the client
It runs faster than the final program
Logic errors can be found before the process is coded
Large processes always fit on one page
It replaces the need for testing

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Flowcharts are visual and language-independent, so errors are found on paper. They can become large, and the program must still be tested.

questions.title: Under 12
questions.text: "Children **under 12** pay a lower price." Which condition is correct for the Yes exit?

scheme.explanation: "Under 12" means 0–11, so 12 itself must take the No exit: age < 12.

questions.title: Iteration
questions.text: What is **iteration** in a flowchart?

options.content: Repeating a group of steps, shown by a flow line going back to an earlier point

scheme.explanation: Iteration = a loop; the arrow goes back to an earlier box, controlled by a decision.

questions.title: Types of loop
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the kind of loop.

prefill: The condition is tested before each repetition; may run zero times
The body always runs at least once

scheme.model_answer: 1 Count-controlled; 2 Pre-condition; 3 Post-condition.
scheme.explanation: FOR repeats a fixed number of times; WHILE tests first (0+ times); REPEAT…UNTIL tests last (at least once).

questions.title: Post-condition loop
questions.text: The body of a REPEAT … UNTIL loop always runs at least once.

scheme.explanation: The condition is tested after the body, so the body runs before the first test.

questions.title: When to use FOR
questions.text: A count-controlled (FOR) loop is the best choice when the user keeps entering values until they type 0.

scheme.explanation: The number of repetitions is not known in advance, so a condition-controlled loop (WHILE or REPEAT) is used.

questions.title: Infinite loop

`count ← 1` · decision `count <= 30?` — Yes: INPUT mark, `total ← total + mark`, back to the decision.

Why does this loop never end?

questions.title: Ticket booking at the Keruen cinema
questions.text:
The **Keruen** cinema in Astana is developing an online booking system. The analyst has drawn a DFD and is now designing each process with flowcharts.

*A ticket costs 2500 ₸; customers under 12 pay 1500 ₸. A booking for **more than 5** tickets gets a 10% discount on the whole booking.*

parts.title: Flowchart
parts.text: Define the term **flowchart**.

scheme.mark_scheme: - a diagram showing the steps of a process / algorithm in order using standard symbols (and arrows) (1)
scheme.model_answer: A diagram that shows the steps of one process in order, using standard symbols joined by flow lines.

parts.title: DFD and flowchart
parts.text: Explain why the analyst draws flowcharts **as well as** the DFD.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the DFD shows what processes there are / how data flows between them (1)
- the flowchart shows how each process works step by step / its decisions and loops, so it can be coded (1)
scheme.model_answer: The DFD only shows which processes exist and the data flowing between them; a flowchart shows how one process works, step by step, so the programmer can code it.

parts.title: Symbols
parts.text: Draw a line to link each step of the booking process to the flowchart symbol used for it.

scheme.mark_scheme: INPUT tickets – parallelogram; discount ← total × 0.1 – rectangle; tickets > 5? – diamond; END – terminator (1 each)
scheme.model_answer: INPUT tickets → parallelogram; discount ← total × 0.1 → rectangle; tickets > 5? → diamond; END → terminator.

parts.title: Conditions
parts.text:
Write the condition used in the decision for each rule.

1. the customer is **under 12**
2. the booking has **more than 5** tickets
3. the age entered is **from 1 to 99** inclusive

scheme.mark_scheme:
1 age < 12 (1)
2 tickets > 5 (1)
3 age >= 1 AND age <= 99 (1) — both limits inclusive and AND
scheme.model_answer: 1 age < 12   2 tickets > 5   3 age >= 1 AND age <= 99

questions.title: Delivery charges at Dala Market
questions.text:
**Dala Market** is an online grocery shop in Karaganda. When an order is placed, the system calculates the amount to pay.

*Orders of **10 000 ₸ or more** are delivered free. Smaller orders pay **1500 ₸** delivery. Customers with a loyalty card get a further **500 ₸** off every order.*

parts.title: Draw the delivery process
parts.text: Draw a flowchart that inputs the order total and whether the customer has a loyalty card (Y/N), calculates the amount to pay and outputs it.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- START / END and INPUT total and card (1)
- decision on total ≥ 10000 (or < 10000) with labelled exits (1)
- delivery 0 / 1500 set on the correct exits (1)
- decision card = "Y" with 500 subtracted on the Yes exit only (1)
- amount = total + delivery (− 500) output after the paths join (1)
scheme.model_answer: START → INPUT total, card → total ≥ 10000? Yes: delivery ← 0; No: delivery ← 1500 → amount ← total + delivery → card = "Y"? Yes: amount ← amount − 500 → OUTPUT amount → END

parts.title: Outputs
parts.text:
State the amount output for each order.

1. total 12 000 ₸, no card
2. total 9 999 ₸, no card
3. total 8 000 ₸, loyalty card

parts.title: Test data
parts.text: Explain why the value **10 000** should be used when testing this flowchart.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- it is a boundary value / the limit of the condition (1)
- it checks that the right operator is used (≥ not >), so 10 000 gets free delivery (1)
scheme.model_answer: 10 000 is the boundary of the rule; testing it shows whether the decision uses ≥ (free delivery, correct) or > (charged, wrong).

questions.title: Totalling at the school canteen
questions.text:
The canteen manager at a school in Aktobe enters the value of each sale at the end of the day. A flowchart of the process contains these steps:

1. `count ← 0`, `total ← 0`
2. `INPUT sale`
3. Decision `sale <> 0?` — No: go to step 7
4. `count ← count + 1`
5. `total ← total + sale`
6. `INPUT sale`, then go back to step 3
7. `OUTPUT count, total`

parts.title: Trace table
parts.text: Complete the trace table for the inputs **700, 1500, 300, 0**. Write one row for each value input (values after the steps that follow it).

parts.title: Type of loop
parts.text: Identify the type of loop used in this flowchart and explain why it is suitable.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- pre-condition / condition-controlled / WHILE loop (1)
- the number of sales is not known in advance / it may be zero, so it stops when 0 is entered (1)
scheme.model_answer: A pre-condition (WHILE) loop: the number of sales is not known in advance and may be zero, so the condition is tested before each repetition.

parts.title: Write the pseudocode
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the same process that also outputs the **average** sale, without dividing by zero.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- initialise count and total to 0 and input the first sale before the loop (1)
- WHILE sale <> 0 … ENDWHILE loop with count + 1 and total + sale inside (1)
- input the next sale inside the loop (1)
- IF count > 0 THEN average ← total / count and output (1)
scheme.model_answer:
count ← 0
total ← 0
INPUT sale
WHILE sale <> 0 DO
    count ← count + 1
    total ← total + sale
    INPUT sale
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT count, total
IF count > 0 THEN
    OUTPUT total / count
ENDIF

questions.title: Registering for the Bilim library app
questions.text:
Students register for the **Bilim** school library app. The registration process inputs a student number and a password.

*The student number must be **from 1000 to 9999**. The password must have **at least 8 characters**. Invalid data is rejected with a message and the student enters it again. Valid data is saved in the Students table and the message "Registered" is shown.*

parts.title: Draw the validation process
parts.text: Draw a flowchart for the registration process.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- INPUT student number and password (1)
- decision 1000 ≤ number ≤ 9999 (with AND) (1)
- decision LENGTH(password) ≥ 8 (1)
- No exits → error message and flow back to the input (1)
- save in the Students table and OUTPUT "Registered", END (1)
scheme.model_answer: START → INPUT number, password → number ≥ 1000 AND number ≤ 9999? No: OUTPUT "Invalid number" → back to INPUT; Yes → LENGTH(password) ≥ 8? No: OUTPUT "Password too short" → back to INPUT; Yes → save in Students → OUTPUT "Registered" → END

parts.title: Validation checks
parts.text:
Name the type of validation check used for

1. the student number
2. the password

scheme.model_answer: 1 Range check   2 Length check

parts.title: Loops for validation
parts.text: The programmer codes the validation with a REPEAT … UNTIL loop. Explain the difference between a pre-condition and a post-condition loop and why a post-condition loop suits validation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- pre-condition: condition tested before the body, may run zero times (1)
- post-condition: tested after the body, runs at least once (1)
- the data must be input at least once before it can be checked, so a post-condition loop fits (1)
scheme.model_answer: A WHILE loop tests first and may not run at all; REPEAT … UNTIL tests after the body, so it always runs once. The data must be entered at least once before it can be checked, so REPEAT … UNTIL (input until valid) suits validation.

questions.title: Issuing a book in the Kitap library system
questions.text:
The **Kitap** library in Pavlodar is getting a new computer system. The analyst has drawn a DFD with the process *Issue book*, which receives *memberID* and *bookID* from the librarian, reads the data stores *Members* and *Books* and writes to the data store *Loans*. The process is now being designed with a flowchart.

*A book can be issued only if the member is registered, has **fewer than 5** books on loan and has **no unpaid fines**, and the book is not already on loan. A loan lasts **14 days**. Unpaid fines are checked by a subroutine `CheckFines`, which is drawn in a separate flowchart.*

parts.title: DFD and flowchart
parts.text: Explain why the analyst draws a flowchart for *Issue book* even though the process already appears on the DFD.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the DFD shows only **what** processes exist / **how data moves** between entities, processes and data stores (1)
- the flowchart shows **how** the process works: the **order of the steps**, the **decisions** (e.g. fewer than 5 loans?) and loops, so the programmer can code it / the tester can plan tests (1)

points.criterion: Flowchart: how, order of steps, decisions, for coding

scheme.model_answer: The DFD only shows that *Issue book* exists and which data flows in and out of it. It does not show the order of the steps or the decisions. The flowchart shows how the process works step by step, including every check (member found? fewer than 5 loans? book available?), so the programmer can code it and the tester can test each path.

parts.title: Symbols
parts.text: Draw a line to link each step of *Issue book* to the flowchart symbol used for it.

scheme.mark_scheme: INPUT memberID, bookID – parallelogram; onLoan < 5? – diamond; CheckFines – rectangle with double vertical sides; dueDate ← today + 14 – rectangle (1 each)
scheme.model_answer: INPUT memberID, bookID → parallelogram (input/output); onLoan < 5? → diamond (decision); CheckFines → rectangle with double vertical sides (subroutine / predefined process); dueDate ← today + 14 → rectangle (process).

parts.title: Draw the Issue book process
parts.text: Draw a flowchart for the process *Issue book*. Each failed check must output a message that says what is wrong and end the process. Call the subroutine `CheckFines` instead of drawing its steps.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- START / END and INPUT memberID, bookID (1)
- decision member found in Members? with No → error message (e.g. "Unknown member") → END (1)
- decision onLoan < 5? (accept onLoan <= 4; not <= 5) with No → "Loan limit reached" → END (1)
- subroutine symbol CheckFines followed by a decision on fines (e.g. fines = 0?) with No → message → END (1)
- decision book available? / not on loan with No → "Book already on loan" → END (1)
- dueDate ← today + 14, save the loan in Loans (data store) and OUTPUT "Return by" dueDate on the path where all checks pass (1)
All decision exits must be labelled Yes / No for the decision marks.

points.criterion: Book available check with error path
Due date, save in Loans, output

scheme.model_answer: START → INPUT memberID, bookID → member in Members? No: OUTPUT "Unknown member" → END; Yes → onLoan < 5? No: OUTPUT "Loan limit reached" → END; Yes → [CheckFines] → fines = 0? No: OUTPUT "Pay fines first" → END; Yes → book available? No: OUTPUT "Book already on loan" → END; Yes → dueDate ← today + 14 → save memberID, bookID, dueDate in Loans → OUTPUT "Return by", dueDate → END
scheme.ai_instructions: The order of the checks may differ, but the member check should come before the others. Do not award the loan-limit mark for onLoan <= 5. Accept a data store shown as a cylinder or as a process box such as 'Save loan in Loans'.

questions.title: Parking charges at the Shymkent Plaza car park
questions.text:
The car park of **Shymkent Plaza** is designing the process that calculates the parking charge when a car leaves.

*Stays of **up to and including 2 hours** are free. Longer stays pay **300 ₸ for every hour** of the stay. The charge is never more than **2000 ₸**. Electric cars park free for any length of time.*

The flowchart inputs `hours` (a whole number) and `electric` (Y/N) and outputs `charge`.

parts.title: Expected outputs
parts.text: State the charge, in ₸, that the process should output for each car (number only).

scheme.model_answer: 1: 0 (2 hours is free); 2: 5 × 300 = 1500; 3: 9 × 300 = 2700, more than the maximum, so 2000.

parts.title: A boundary error
parts.text: The programmer drew the first decision as `hours < 2?` (Yes → charge ← 0). Explain the error and identify the test data that would show it.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the condition should be `hours <= 2` / 2 hours must be free, but `hours < 2` sends 2 hours to the paid path (1)
- test with the boundary value hours = 2 (electric N): expected 0, the flowchart outputs 600 (1)

points.criterion: Test data 2 with expected / actual output

scheme.model_answer: `hours < 2` is false for exactly 2 hours, so a 2-hour stay is charged 2 × 300 = 600 ₸ instead of being free; the condition should be `hours <= 2`. The boundary value hours = 2 shows the error: the expected output is 0 but the flowchart gives 600.

parts.title: A wrong condition
parts.text: The car park wants to count the cars that stayed **from 3 to 6 hours**. Which condition is **true for every** value of `hours`?

scheme.model_answer: C — hours >= 3 OR hours <= 6.
scheme.explanation: With OR only one part needs to be true: every number is either at least 3 or at most 6. A, B and D are all correct ways of writing 'from 3 to 6'.

parts.title: Electric cars first
parts.text: Explain why the decision `electric = "Y"?` should be placed **before** the decisions about hours in the flowchart.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- an electric car is free whatever the hours, so the other checks are not needed for it / the check that makes the others pointless goes first (1)
- otherwise the electric car could be given a charge on the hours path / the paths would need extra checks to set the charge back to 0 (1)

points.criterion: Other checks pointless for electric cars

scheme.model_answer: If the car is electric the charge is 0 whatever the number of hours, so checking the hours would be pointless. Putting this decision first sends electric cars straight to charge ← 0 and stops them being charged on the hours path.

questions.title: Step counter in the Qadam fitness app
questions.text:
The **Qadam** fitness app records the number of steps a user walks on each of the **5** school days of a week. A flowchart of the weekly summary contains these steps:

1. `total ← 0`, `goal ← 0`, `day ← 1`
2. Decision `day <= 5?` — No: go to step 8
3. `INPUT steps`
4. `total ← total + steps`
5. Decision `steps >= 10000?` — Yes: `goal ← goal + 1`
6. `day ← day + 1`
7. Go back to step 2
8. `OUTPUT total, goal`

parts.title: Trace table
parts.text: Complete the trace table for the inputs **8000, 12000, 10000, 9999, 15000**. Write one row for each value input: the value of `day` when it is input, and the values of `total` and `goal` after steps 4 and 5.

parts.title: Type of loop
parts.text: Identify the type of loop used in this flowchart and explain why it is suitable for this process.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- count-controlled loop (FOR loop) (1)
- the number of repetitions (5 days) is known before the loop starts (1)

points.criterion: Number of days known in advance

scheme.model_answer: It is a count-controlled loop: a counter `day` goes from 1 to 5. It is suitable because the number of repetitions — 5 school days — is known before the loop starts.

parts.title: Write the pseudocode
parts.text: Write pseudocode for the same process using a `FOR` loop. It must also output the **average** number of steps per day.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- total ← 0 and goal ← 0 before a FOR day ← 1 TO 5 … NEXT loop (1)
- INPUT steps and total ← total + steps inside the loop (1)
- IF steps >= 10000 THEN goal ← goal + 1 inside the loop, and OUTPUT total, goal and total / 5 after the loop (1)

points.criterion: Input and totalling in the loop
Counting decision and outputs incl. average after the loop

scheme.model_answer:
total ← 0
goal ← 0
FOR day ← 1 TO 5
    INPUT steps
    total ← total + steps
    IF steps >= 10000 THEN
        goal ← goal + 1
    ENDIF
NEXT day
OUTPUT total, goal
OUTPUT total / 5
scheme.ai_instructions: Any clear pseudocode or code is acceptable. The average may be total / 5 or total / day-count; outputs must be after the loop for the last mark.

questions.title: Entering marks in the Kundelik e-diary
questions.text: A teacher enters each student's mark for a test into a school e-diary. The mark must be a **whole number from 1 to 10**. An invalid mark is rejected with a message and the teacher enters it again. A valid mark is saved in the *Marks* table and the message *Saved* is output.

parts.title: Draw the validation process
parts.text: Draw a flowchart for entering **one** mark, using a **post-condition** loop for the validation.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- START / END and INPUT mark placed inside the loop (1)

blocks.content: In the **design** stage of a new system the analyst already has a **DFD**, which shows **what** processes the system has (e.g. *Register client*, *Calculate order cost*). Before anything is coded, each process is designed in detail: **how** it works, step by step. The most common tool for this is the **flowchart** — the programmer later turns it into code.

blocks.text: Where process design fits in the life cycle

blocks.content: A new system is developed in stages: **analysis** (finding out what the client needs), **design** (planning how the system will meet those needs), **development** (coding), **testing**, **implementation** and **maintenance**. Design itself has several parts. **Data design** plans the tables, fields and data types of the database. **Interface design** plans the screens, forms and reports. **Process design** plans the **logic** — what the computer must do, in which order, with which decisions — for every process that appears in the DFD.

Think of a school canteen system. The DFD has a process *Record sale*. It tells us that the cashier sends *items chosen* into the process and that the process writes to the data store *Sales*. It does **not** tell us what happens when a student's card has too little money on it, how the total is calculated, or when a receipt is printed. Those details are exactly what process design adds. Without them, two programmers given the same DFD could write two systems that behave differently — and neither of them might behave the way the canteen manager wanted.
Process design therefore answers four questions for every process:

items: **What are the inputs?** — data typed by a user, read from a sensor, or read from a file or database.
**What processing is done?** — calculations, comparisons, assignments, searching and sorting.
**What decisions and repetitions are there?** — the conditions that choose a path and the steps that must be repeated.
**What are the outputs?** — data displayed, printed, sent to another device or saved to a data store.

blocks.content: This is the **input → process → output** (IPO) model. A good flowchart makes each of these four parts visible, so the client, the programmer and the tester can all check them.

A **diagram** that shows the **steps of a process (algorithm) in order**, using **standard symbols** joined by **flow lines (arrows)**. It shows the **inputs, processing, decisions, loops and outputs** of one process.
A **finite sequence of clear steps** that solves a problem or carries out a task. A flowchart and pseudocode are two ways of **representing** an algorithm.

The part of system design in which the **logic of every process** of the new system is planned (with flowcharts or pseudocode), so that it can be **coded, tested and checked** with the client before development starts.

blocks.caption: The standard flowchart symbols

blocks.content: Flowcharts are useful only because everybody draws them **the same way**. A programmer in Almaty and a tester in Shymkent must read a diamond as a decision without having to ask. That is why the shapes are **standard** and why examiners give no mark for a step drawn in the wrong shape.

items: The **terminator** is a rounded rectangle (often called an oval). It appears at the very beginning with the word **START** and at the end with **END** (or **STOP**). A flowchart for a subroutine may start with its name, e.g. `CalculateTax`, and end with **RETURN**. There is exactly one start, so a reader always knows where to begin.

The **process** box is a plain rectangle. It holds one action that the computer carries out internally: an **assignment** (`count ← 0`), a **calculation** (`cost ← tickets × 2500`) or a change to a variable (`i ← i + 1`). Nothing is typed by the user and nothing is shown on the screen in a process box.

The **input / output** box is a parallelogram. It is used whenever data **crosses the boundary** of the computer: the user types something (`INPUT pin`), a sensor value is read (`INPUT temperature`), or something is displayed or printed (`OUTPUT "Card blocked"`). Write `INPUT` or `OUTPUT` in the box, so that the reader can tell which direction the data moves.

The **decision** box is a diamond. It holds a **question whose answer is Yes or No** (True or False), such as `balance >= price?`. It always has **two** exits, and both are labelled. A diamond never contains an action — it only chooses which path is followed next.

The **subroutine** (predefined process) is a rectangle with double vertical sides. It means "carry out a process that is drawn in a separate flowchart". Large systems use subroutines to keep each flowchart small: the checkout flowchart can simply call `CalculateDelivery` instead of drawing all of its steps again.
The **flow line** is an arrow. It shows the **order** in which the steps are carried out. Lines normally run from top to bottom; a line that goes **back up** creates a loop (lesson 2).

blocks.text: From a DFD process to a flowchart

blocks.content: A DFD and a flowchart are not competitors: they are used **one after the other**. The analyst first draws the DFD to agree with the client **which** processes the system needs and which data each process uses. Then every process circle (or rounded box) of the DFD is taken in turn and a flowchart is drawn for it. The **data flows into the process** become the **inputs** of the flowchart; the **data flows out** become its **outputs**; a **data store** the process reads or writes becomes a "read from" or "save to" step. The DFD shows the system **from above**, the flowchart shows **one process from inside**.

For example, the clinic DFD process *Book appointment* has the flows *patient ID* and *preferred date* coming in from the external entity *Patient*, reads the data store *Timetable* and writes to *Appointments*. Its flowchart starts with `INPUT patientID, date`, checks `doctor free on date?`, saves the appointment if the answer is Yes and outputs a confirmation, or outputs "No free slot" if the answer is No.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages of flowcharts
rows: **Visual** — the logic is easy to follow, even for a non-programmer (the client)
Errors in the logic are found **before coding**
**Slow** to draw and to change — a small change may mean redrawing
Not as close to code as pseudocode
Becomes part of the **technical documentation** for maintenance
Complex conditions are hard to fit into a diamond

blocks.content: The main reason is **cost**. A mistake in the logic — for example, giving the discount to customers who should not get it — is cheap to fix while it is still a drawing: you rub out one arrow. The same mistake found after the program is written means changing code and testing again; found after the system is **installed**, it may mean wrong bills sent to hundreds of customers. The earlier an error is found, the cheaper it is to correct.

A second reason is **communication**. A client usually cannot read Python or PHP, but can follow a flowchart and say "No, members of staff get the discount too". A third reason is **testing**: every decision in the flowchart shows a path that must be tested, so the tester can plan **test data** for each Yes and No exit, including the **boundary** values. Finally, the flowcharts become part of the **technical documentation**; a programmer who has to change the system two years later can understand each process without reading every line of code.

- **One START** and at least one **END**.
- Flow from **top to bottom** (and left to right); every flow line has an **arrowhead**.
- Every **decision** has exactly **two exits**, labelled **Yes / No** (or True / False).
- **One step per box**, written clearly — e.g. `INPUT price`, not "the user types something".
- Use the **correct symbol** for each step.
- A loop returns to a point **before** the decision (or body) it repeats.
- No flow line ends in mid-air; avoid crossing lines.

- Drawing an **input or output** in a **rectangle**, or a **calculation** in a **parallelogram**.
- Forgetting **START** or **END**, or using a rectangle for them.
- Writing a whole paragraph in one box instead of one step per box.
- Saying that a flowchart "shows the data flow of the whole system" — that is a **DFD**.
Every algorithm is built from only **three** structures: **sequence**, **selection** and **iteration** (lesson 2).

In a **sequence** the computer carries out each step **once**, in the order written. The order is not decoration: changing it changes the result. If a process first outputs `cost` and only then calculates `cost ← tickets × 2500`, the output is empty or out of date. A classic exam trap is swapping two variables: `a ← b` followed by `b ← a` leaves both variables equal to the old `b`, because the old value of `a` was overwritten. The correct sequence uses a **temporary variable**: `temp ← a`, `a ← b`, `b ← temp`. When you design a sequence, ask for each step: *does every value it uses already exist at this point?*

blocks.text: Selection — one path or the other

blocks.content: **Selection** lets a process react to its data. The diamond asks a question, and the answer decides which branch runs. There are three common patterns:

items: **IF … THEN … ELSE** — two different actions, one for Yes and one for No (cinema: child price or adult price).
**IF … THEN** with no ELSE — an action happens only when the condition is true; the No exit goes straight to the joining point (add a 10 % discount only if the customer has a loyalty card).
**Nested IF** — a second decision placed on one exit of the first, used when there are **more than two** outcomes (grades A, B, C, Fail).

blocks.content: In every pattern the branches **join again** before the process continues, so the flowchart still has a single route to END. In pseudocode the join is the `ENDIF`.

Conditions are built from **comparison operators** (`=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`) and **logical operators** (`AND`, `OR`, `NOT`). The most frequent errors are at **boundaries**. "Under 12" is `age < 12` (12 is not under 12); "12 or over" is `age >= 12`; "from 11 to 18 inclusive" is `age >= 11 AND age <= 18`. Always test a decision with a value just below, exactly on, and just above each boundary — this is called **boundary testing**.

When two conditions must both be true, you can either write one diamond with `AND` or draw **two nested diamonds**: the second question is asked only on the Yes exit of the first, and both No exits lead to the same action. The two designs are **equivalent** — they give the same output for every input. Nested diamonds are easier to read when each condition needs its **own error message** ("too young", "too old"); one diamond with `AND` is shorter when one message is enough.
Steps carried out **one after another, in order**, each exactly once. In a flowchart: a straight line of boxes from START to END.

A **decision** chooses which path to follow, depending on whether a **condition** is **true or false**. In a flowchart: a **diamond** with two exits (Yes / No) that **join again** later. In pseudocode: `IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF`.
A **variable** is a named storage location whose value can change (e.g. `cost`). **Assignment** `cost ← tickets × 2500` stores the value on the right in the variable on the left.

blocks.title: How to draw a flowchart from a description
items: Read the task and list the **inputs**, the **outputs** and the **calculations**.
Find every **condition** ("if", "more than", "only when") → each becomes a **decision**.
Find every **repetition** ("for each", "until", "keep asking") → a **loop** (lesson 2).
Draw **START**, then the boxes **top to bottom**, one step per box, with the correct symbols.
Label the two exits of every decision **Yes / No** and make the paths **join** again.
Finish with **END**, then **trace** it with test data (normal, boundary, invalid).

- A decision with **one exit** only, or exits not labelled Yes / No.
- Writing the decision as a statement (`age = 12`) when a **question** is meant (`age = 12?`), or putting an assignment in a diamond.
- Wrong boundary: "under 12" is `age < 12`, not `age <= 12`; "from 11 to 18" needs `>=` and `<=`.
- Using `OR` where `AND` is needed: `age >= 11 OR age <= 18` is true for **every** age.
- Forgetting to **join** the two paths, so one path has no END.

theory.title: Flowcharts of processes in computing systems

blocks.content: The learning objective asks you to **develop flowcharts of processes in computing systems**. In the exam this means: you are given a short description of a real system — a library, a shop, a vending machine, a school portal — and you must turn **one of its processes** into a correct flowchart. This section shows how real processes are structured and how to go from the words of a scenario to a finished diagram.

A set of steps that the system carries out to **turn inputs into outputs** for one task — e.g. *Issue book*, *Calculate bill*, *Log in*. In a DFD it is one process box; in process design it gets its own flowchart.

A **named block of steps** designed and drawn **separately** and then **called** from another flowchart with the double-sided rectangle. It avoids drawing the same steps twice and keeps each flowchart small.

A step in which the process **reads data from** or **saves data to** a file or database table, e.g. *Save loan in Loans*. Some books draw it as a cylinder, others as a process box with the words "read" / "save".

blocks.text: What real processes have in common

blocks.content: Almost every process in an information system follows the same pattern. First it **collects input** — from a form, a barcode scanner, a card reader or a sensor. Then it **checks** that input: does the customer exist, is the value in range, is there enough money or stock? Each check is a **decision**, and each No exit usually ends with an **error message** so that the user knows what went wrong. Only when every check is passed does the process do its real work: **calculate**, **update the database** and **output** a result such as a receipt or a confirmation. Designers call this the "guard checks first" pattern: put the checks at the top, so the main work runs only on good data.

A second common feature is that processes **read and write stored data**. A cash machine reads the account balance and writes the new balance; a library reads the member's record and writes a new loan. In the flowchart these appear as clear, separate steps, so the programmer knows exactly when the database is used.

A third feature is that processes often **call other processes**. The checkout of an online shop calls *Calculate delivery*, *Take payment* and *Send e-mail*. Each of these is a **subroutine** with its own flowchart. This is called **top-down design** or **decomposition**: a big problem is split into smaller sub-problems that are each easy to draw, code and test, and different programmers can work on different subroutines at the same time.

:::example Worked example — issuing a book in the school library
*The school library lends books to registered students. A student may have at most **5** books at a time. A book can be issued only if it is not already on loan. A loan lasts **14 days**. Design the process* Issue book.

1. **Inputs:** the librarian scans the student card and the book → `INPUT memberID, bookID`.
2. **Checks (decisions)**, in a sensible order: is the member in the Members table? Does the member have fewer than 5 books (`onLoan < 5?`)? Is the book available? Each No exit outputs a message that says **what** is wrong and ends the process.
3. **Processing:** `dueDate ← today + 14`.
4. **Data store:** the loan (memberID, bookID, dueDate) is saved in the *Loans* table.
5. **Output:** "Return by" and the due date.
6. **Test plan:** one test for every exit — an unknown card, a member with 5 books (boundary: 4 books → allowed, 5 → refused), a book already on loan, and a normal loan.

The order of the checks matters for the user: there is no point checking the book if the card is unknown.

blocks.title: Worked example — a drinks vending machine
blocks.content:
*A vending machine sells a drink for **300 ₸**. The customer chooses a drink and inserts money. If the money is less than the price the machine shows "Insert more" and returns the money. If the chosen drink is sold out it shows "Sold out" and returns the money. Otherwise it gives the drink, reduces the stock by 1 and gives change.*

1. Inputs: `INPUT choice`, `INPUT paid`.
2. Decision 1: `stock[choice] > 0?` — No → OUTPUT "Sold out", return `paid` → END.
3. Decision 2: `paid >= 300?` — No → OUTPUT "Insert more", return `paid` → END.
4. Processing: `stock[choice] ← stock[choice] − 1`, `change ← paid − 300`.
5. Outputs: give the drink, OUTPUT `change`, END.
6. Test with `paid` = 299 (refused), 300 (change 0) and 500 (change 200), and with a sold-out drink.

The boundary value 300 must be **accepted** — so the condition is `>=`, not `>`.

blocks.title: Exam-style questions with model answers
blocks.content:
**Q: State the purpose of a flowchart in the design stage of a new system. [2]**
It shows **how a process works step by step** / the order of inputs, processes, decisions and outputs (1), so that the logic can be checked and the **programmer can code it** (1).

**Q: Name the flowchart symbol used for `INPUT quantity` and the symbol used for `quantity > 10?`. [2]**
Parallelogram (input/output) (1); diamond (decision) (1).

**Q: A shop charges 1500 ₸ delivery for orders under 10 000 ₸; larger orders are delivered free. Draw a flowchart that inputs the order total and outputs the amount to pay. [4]**
INPUT total (1); decision `total >= 10000?` / `total < 10000?` with Yes/No labels (1); correct delivery on each exit (0 or 1500) (1); OUTPUT total + delivery, paths joined and START/END present (1).

**Q: Give the output of the grade flowchart (85 / 70 / 50 boundaries) for the marks 70 and 49. [2]**
70 → "B" (1); 49 → "Fail" (1).

**Q: Explain why the condition `age >= 11 OR age <= 18` is wrong for "ages 11 to 18". [2]**
With OR only one part has to be true (1), so every age (e.g. 40, since 40 ≥ 11) gives Yes; `AND` is needed (1).

- Naming shapes incorrectly: the **diamond** is a decision, the **parallelogram** is input/output, the **oval** is the terminator.
- Drawing a flowchart with no labels on the decision exits — examiners do not give the decision mark.
- Describing what the flowchart is "about" instead of giving the **output** for the input asked.

blocks.content: Computers are most useful when the same steps must be done **many times**: marking 850 attendance records, adding up every sale of the day, asking for a password until it is right. Without iteration a flowchart for 850 students would need 850 copies of the same boxes. With a loop the steps are drawn **once** and an arrow sends the flow back to repeat them. Every loop has four parts, and an examiner looks for all of them:

items: **Initialisation** — variables are given starting values **before** the loop (`count ← 0`, `i ← 1`).
**The loop condition** — a decision that says whether to repeat again or to leave the loop.
**The body** — the steps that are repeated (input, calculate, update).
**The update** — something inside the body changes, so that the condition eventually becomes true (or false) and the loop **ends**. If nothing changes, the loop never stops: an **infinite loop**.

blocks.content: **Repeating** a group of steps (the **loop body**) — either a **fixed** number of times or **until / while a condition** is met. In a flowchart a loop is a **flow line going back** to an earlier point, controlled by a **decision**.
A loop that repeats a **known, fixed number of times**, using a **counter** (`FOR i ← 1 TO 30 … NEXT i`).

A loop that repeats **while** a condition is true (**pre-condition**, tested **before** the body: `WHILE … ENDWHILE`) or **until** a condition becomes true (**post-condition**, tested **after** the body: `REPEAT … UNTIL`). Used when the number of repetitions is **not known in advance**.

blocks.title: Three kinds of loop
rows: Process every student of a class of 25
**0 or more** times, **while** the condition is true
Read orders while there are more
**At least once**, **until** the condition is true
Ask for a PIN until it is correct

blocks.content: A **count-controlled loop** is used when the number of repetitions is **known before the loop starts** — 25 students in a class, 12 months in a year, 10 items in a list. A counter variable `i` starts at 1, the decision asks `i <= 25?`, the body runs, and `i ← i + 1` is the last step before the arrow goes back to the decision. In pseudocode the `FOR … NEXT` statement does the setting, testing and increasing automatically, but in a flowchart all three must be **drawn**. The number of repetitions can also come from an input: `INPUT n`, then `FOR i ← 1 TO n` — it is still count-controlled, because `n` is known when the loop begins.

A **pre-condition loop** (`WHILE`) asks its question **before** each run of the body. If the condition is false at the very start, the body is **skipped completely** — it runs zero times. That makes it the safe choice when there may be nothing to process: the canteen may have had no sales, a file may be empty. In the flowchart the diamond comes **first** and the arrow from the end of the body goes **back up to the diamond**. Note the typical "read ahead" pattern: the first value is input **before** the loop, and the next value is input at the **end** of the body, so the condition always tests a fresh value.

A **post-condition loop** (`REPEAT … UNTIL`) runs the body **first** and asks its question **afterwards**, so the body always runs **at least once**. It suits processes where the user must do something before there is anything to check — entering a PIN, choosing a menu option, entering a value that is then validated. In the flowchart the body comes first, then the diamond, and the **No** exit (condition not yet met) goes back up to the start of the body. Remember the logic is reversed compared with WHILE: `WHILE` repeats **while the condition is true**, `REPEAT … UNTIL` repeats **until the condition becomes true**.

blocks.content: A **counter** starts at **0** and increases by **1** each time an event happens: `count ← count + 1` — e.g. the number of late students.
A **total** starts at **0** and the **value** of each item is added: `total ← total + price` — e.g. the total value of the day's orders.

Counting and totalling are the two "accumulator" patterns that appear in nearly every exam flowchart. Both variables must be set to **0 before the loop** — if they were set inside the loop, they would be reset to 0 on every repetition and the final answer would only describe the last item. The counter is increased by a **fixed 1**; the total is increased by the **value** of the current item. The **average** is calculated **after** the loop, as `total / count`, and only if `count > 0`, otherwise the program would divide by zero.

A related pattern is finding the **largest** (or smallest) value. A variable `max` is set to the **first** value (or to a value lower than any possible one), and inside the loop a decision `value > max?` replaces `max` when a bigger value appears. Setting `max ← 0` is a trap when all values can be negative, such as winter temperatures in Astana.

blocks.title: Worked example — the school canteen
blocks.content:
*At the end of the day the canteen manager enters the value of each sale. Entering **0** means there are no more sales. The process outputs the **number of sales**, the **total takings** and the **average** sale.*

1. The number of sales is not known → a **condition-controlled** loop.
2. **Initialise** before the loop: `count ← 0`, `total ← 0`.
3. `INPUT sale` **before** the loop, then `WHILE sale <> 0`: `count ← count + 1`, `total ← total + sale`, `INPUT sale` again.
4. After the loop: if `count > 0` then `average ← total / count`; OUTPUT count, total, average.
5. Test with 800, 1200, 600, 0 → count = 3, total = 2600, average ≈ 866.67. Test with just 0 → count = 0 and **no division by zero** — this is why the pre-condition loop and the extra check are used.

blocks.title: Worked example — the coldest morning of the week
blocks.content:
*A weather station in Astana records the temperature at 7:00 on each of the **7** days of a week. Design a process that outputs the **lowest** temperature and the **number of days below −20 °C**.*

1. Seven readings, known in advance → **count-controlled** loop, `FOR day ← 1 TO 7`.
2. Before the loop: `cold ← 0`. The lowest value cannot start at 0 (all readings may be below 0), so input the **first** reading before the loop and set `min ← temp`, then loop for days 2 to 7 — or start `min` at a very large number such as 100.
3. In the body: `INPUT temp`; decision `temp < min?` → Yes: `min ← temp`; decision `temp < −20?` → Yes: `cold ← cold + 1`.
4. After the loop: `OUTPUT min, cold`.
5. Trace with −18, −25, −22, −15, −30, −19, −21: min = −30, cold = 4 (−25, −22, −30, −21).

Notice the two separate decisions: one updates the minimum, the other counts — they are independent, so neither is placed on the exit of the other.

- **Initialising** the counter or total **inside** the loop — it is reset every time.
- Forgetting to **change** the counter (`i ← i + 1`) → an **infinite loop**.
- An **off-by-one** error: `i < 850` instead of `i <= 850` processes only 849 students.
- Using a FOR loop when the number of repetitions is **not known** (e.g. "until the user enters 0").
- Confusing counting (`+ 1`) with totalling (`+ value`).
Many processes of a system must **validate input** before it is stored: the flowchart **keeps asking** until the data obeys the rule, so wrong data never reaches the database.

Validation matters because a database is only as good as the data in it — "garbage in, garbage out". If a school system accepts a mark of 95 on a 10-point scale, every average, report and ranking calculated from it will be wrong, and nobody may notice for weeks. It is far cheaper to stop bad data **at the moment it is entered**, while the user is still at the keyboard and can correct it, than to find and fix it later.

In a flowchart a validation process is a **loop**: input → check → if wrong, explain and ask again. It can be drawn in two ways. With a **post-condition** loop the input is inside the loop and the condition "data valid?" is tested after it; the error message is output on the No path before going back. With a **pre-condition** loop the data is input once before the loop, and the loop `WHILE data invalid` outputs the message and inputs again. Both give the same behaviour; the important points are that the error message **explains the problem** ("Age must be from 11 to 18", not just "Error") and that the flow **returns to the input** rather than ending.

A process often needs **several checks** on the same data or on several fields. Each check is its own diamond, so that each failure can give its **own message**. The checks run in order — usually presence first (is anything there?), then type, then length / format, then range — because there is no point checking the range of an empty field. Many real systems also limit the number of attempts (three wrong PINs block a card), which combines a validation loop with a **counter**.

An **automatic check by the computer** that input data is **sensible / reasonable and obeys the rules** (e.g. within a range, in the right format) **before** it is accepted. It cannot prove that the data is **correct** — only that it is allowed.

blocks.title: How to build a validation loop
items: **Input** the data.
**Decision**: does it obey the rule (range, presence, length, format, type)?
**No** → **output an error message** that says what is wrong, and flow **back to the input**.
**Yes** → continue with the next step (store, calculate, output).
**Test** it with **normal**, **boundary** (11, 18) and **erroneous** (10, 19, "abc") data.

blocks.content: **Verification** is not the same as validation. Validation asks "is this data allowed?"; verification asks "is this data the **same** as the original?". A double-entry verification is easy to draw as a flowchart: `INPUT password`, `INPUT confirm`, decision `password = confirm?` — No → "Passwords do not match" and back to the first input. A system that needs reliable data uses **both**: the password is first validated (at least 8 characters), then verified (typed twice).

blocks.content:
- After the error message the flow goes to **END** — the user must be asked **again**.
- The error-message path joins **after** the decision instead of **before the input**.
- A range check written with `OR` (`age >= 11 OR age <= 18`) — it accepts every age.
- Claiming that validation makes data **correct** — a valid age 15 can still be the wrong age.

A table with **one column per variable** (and for conditions / outputs), filled in **row by row** as the flowchart or algorithm is followed **by hand** with test data. It is used to find the **output** and to find **logic errors**.

A flowchart can look correct and still be wrong. **Tracing** (a **dry run**) is the way to find out before anything is coded: you play the part of the computer, follow the arrows one box at a time and write down every value in a **trace table**. Tracing finds **logic errors** — mistakes where the flowchart runs but gives the wrong answer, such as a wrong boundary, a counter that is never increased or an output in the wrong place. It is also how exam questions ask you to show that you understand an algorithm: "Complete the trace table for the input data …".

Choose the test data carefully. **Normal** data checks the usual path; **boundary** data (the values exactly at the limits, e.g. 8:30) checks that every `<` and `<=` is right; **erroneous** data checks the validation paths. When the expected output (worked out by hand from the task) differs from the traced output, the row where they first differ shows where the error is.

blocks.title: How to trace a flowchart
items: Write a column for **every variable**, plus columns for important **conditions** and the **output**.
Fill in the **initial values** (e.g. `total = 0`) in the first row.
Follow the arrows one box at a time; write a **new value only when a variable changes**.
At each **decision** write the result (Yes / No) and follow that exit.
Stop at **END**; the output column is the answer.

blocks.content: Converting between a flowchart and pseudocode is mechanical once you recognise the **shape** of each structure. Look first for arrows that go **back up** — each of them is a loop. If the diamond comes **before** the body, it is a `WHILE`; if the body comes **before** the diamond, it is a `REPEAT … UNTIL`; if a counter is set, compared and increased, it is a `FOR`. Every diamond whose two paths **join further down** without going back is an `IF`. The remaining parallelograms become `INPUT` / `OUTPUT` and the rectangles become assignments. When converting a `REPEAT … UNTIL` from pseudocode, check the exit label: the loop ends when the `UNTIL` condition is **true**, so the **Yes** exit leaves the loop and the **No** exit goes back.

blocks.title: Flowchart ↔ pseudocode
rows: Diamond with Yes / No exits that join again
Diamond **before** the body + arrow back **up** to the diamond
Body **before** the diamond + arrow back **up** to the body
Counter set, compared with a limit, increased, arrow back

blocks.title: Worked example — converting pseudocode into a flowchart
blocks.content:
```text | A PIN check (at most 3 tries)
tries ← 0
REPEAT
    INPUT pin
    tries ← tries + 1
UNTIL pin = 4321 OR tries = 3
IF pin = 4321 THEN
    OUTPUT "Welcome"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Card blocked"
ENDIF
```
1. `tries ← 0` → **process** box after START.
2. `REPEAT` → nothing is drawn; remember **where the loop starts** (the next box).
3. `INPUT pin` → **parallelogram**; `tries ← tries + 1` → **rectangle**.
4. `UNTIL …` → **diamond** `pin = 4321 OR tries = 3?`; **No** → arrow back up to `INPUT pin`.
5. **Yes** → second **diamond** `pin = 4321?` → Yes: OUTPUT "Welcome"; No: OUTPUT "Card blocked"; join → END.

- In a trace table, rewriting **every** variable on every row — write a value only when it **changes**, but do not skip a change.
- Forgetting the **last test** of the loop condition (the row where the loop ends).
- Converting a post-condition loop into `WHILE` — the body would then not be guaranteed to run once.
- Mixing up the arrow targets: the loop arrow goes **back up**, the exit goes **on** to the next step.

blocks.title: Exam-style questions with model answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe the difference between a pre-condition loop and a post-condition loop. [2]**
A pre-condition loop tests the condition **before** the body, so the body may run **zero** times (1); a post-condition loop tests **after** the body, so it always runs **at least once** (1).

**Q: Draw a flowchart that inputs the prices of 10 items and outputs the total. [5]**
`total ← 0` (and counter set) before the loop (1); loop for 10 items with a decision / counter (1); INPUT price inside the loop (1); `total ← total + price` (1); OUTPUT total after the loop, START/END (1).

**Q: Draw a flowchart for a registration process that validates the e-mail (contains "@" and ".") and the password (at least 8 characters), stores the data and shows a confirmation. [5]**
Input of the data (1); e-mail decision (1); password decision (1); invalid data → error message and **back to input** (1); store in the database and output a confirmation (1).

**Q: State the output of this algorithm: `n ← 1`, `REPEAT n ← n × 2 UNTIL n > 20`, `OUTPUT n`. [1]**
32 (1) — n takes the values 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.

**Q: Explain why the canteen process (sales until 0 is entered) uses a condition-controlled loop and not a count-controlled loop. [2]**
The number of sales is **not known in advance** (1), so the loop must stop when a condition (sale = 0) is met, not after a fixed count (1).

- A loop with no **decision** — the examiner cannot see when it stops.
- Output **inside** the loop when only the final total is asked for.
- A validation flowchart whose error path ends at END instead of returning to the input.
